results.result: AMATERAS-2 is a volumetric trans-scale imaging system with a custom-made giant lens (×2 magnification, NA=0.25) that achieves ~1.1 µm transverse resolution across a ~1.5×1.0 cm² FOV using optical and computational sectioning techniques.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 describe the core technical specifications and capabilities of AMATERAS-2. The system specifications (C2, C3) are explicitly stated and the 3D capability (C4) is demonstrated through experimental results in subsequent claims. These foundational claims are well-supported by the detailed methods and experimental validation.

results.result: The AMATERAS-2 lens system consists of a 12-element objective lens (144×310 mm) and 9-element tube lens (170×345 mm), both infinity-corrected with NAs of 0.25 and 0.125 respectively, a 44 mm field number, and aberration correction to the diffraction limit across 436-656 nm with zero vignetting.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C22 provide detailed optical specifications of the lens system that are explicitly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1. These are design specifications from the manufacturer and represent verifiable technical parameters of the custom-made lens system.

results.result: AMATERAS-2 theoretically achieves over 2× transverse resolution, over 4× longitudinal resolution, and over 4× brightness compared to AMATERAS-1 based on the doubled NA (0.25 vs 0.12).
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25 present theoretical predictions based on optical principles relating NA to resolution and brightness. These are standard optical relationships (resolution ∝ 1/NA, axial resolution ∝ 1/NA², brightness ∝ NA²) and are later validated experimentally in C28-C29, C32-C33, and C36.

results.result: AMATERAS-2 uses either a 120-megapixel (2.2 µm pixel) or 250-megapixel (1.5 µm pixel) CMOS camera, achieving measured transverse resolutions of 1.24±0.12 µm and 1.12±0.072 µm respectively, with DOFs of 15.6±1.3 µm and 14.8±1.1 µm, where DOF differences are attributed to pixel size.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C34 describe camera specifications and experimentally measured PSF characteristics with N=100 measurements. The measurements are well-documented with error bars and the interpretation of DOF differences (C34) is supported by citation. The measured resolutions are close to theoretical predictions.

results.result: AMATERAS-2w achieves approximately 2× improved transverse resolution compared to AMATERAS-1, delivering more detailed images with finer spatial structures including sharper visualization of filamentous actin and enabling observation of subcellular structures like myofibrils in large-area cell sheets.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C39 describe the practical imaging improvements demonstrated in Figure 2C-F comparing AMATERAS-2w to AMATERAS-1. The 2× improvement matches theoretical predictions (C23) and is visually demonstrated with line profile comparisons showing sharper features.

results.result: The confocal method was selected as most compatible with AMATERAS-2 because light-sheet microscopy struggles with uniform illumination at centimeter scale, light-field microscopy involves resolution trade-offs incompatible with AMATERAS's concept, two-photon microscopy requires further innovations for wide FOV, and standard microlens-pinhole arrays are incompatible with the large tube lens NA (0.125).
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C44 provide the rationale for choosing the confocal approach with supporting citations. The technical reasoning about incompatibility of standard microlens arrays (C44) is sound given the large NA, and the limitations of alternative methods are appropriately cited.

results.result: A custom pinhole array disk (6 µm pinholes, 24 µm spacing) dramatically suppresses out-of-focus background and achieves optical sectioning. With ×1 relay lens (NA=0.079), transverse resolution degrades but longitudinal FWHM is ~16 µm; with ×2 relay lens (NA=0.12), transverse degradation is smaller and longitudinal FWHM is ~14 µm, both exceeding the ideal ~9.5 µm due to loose excitation focusing and non-negligible pinhole size.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C51 describe the confocal system design and measured performance shown in Figure 3. The dramatic background suppression (C46) is visually demonstrated in Figure 3C. The measured PSF characteristics (C50) with N=100 are well-documented, and the interpretation of discrepancies from ideal values (C51) is reasonable.

results.result: A computational sectioning method was developed that estimates out-of-focus contributions by iterative low-pass filtering, assuming higher spatial frequency in the focal plane. Applied to myocardial organoids, it clearly visualizes cTnT and nuclei distribution in each z-layer, revealing a hollow oval structure of cTnT-positive cardiomyocytes over cTnT-negative cells. The method is effective when fluorescent molecules are localized or filament-like and requires uniform, clearly higher spatial frequency in the focal plane.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C57 describe the computational sectioning algorithm and its validation on myocardial organoids (Figure 4). The method is clearly explained, the results (C54-C55) are demonstrated in Figure 4D-E with consistency to prior literature (Ma et al., 2015), and the limitations/assumptions (C56-C57) are appropriately stated.

results.result: AMATERAS-2 successfully imaged a 1.5-mm-thick CUBIC-cleared mouse brain section with SYTOX-Green staining, acquiring 378 layers at 4 µm steps with 1 s exposure. Computational sectioning eliminated background light enabling clear images even in high-background areas, and ×4 magnification improved spatial resolution and cell separation in both xy and xz planes compared to ×2.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C62 describe the mouse brain imaging experiment shown in Figure 5. The experimental parameters (C59-C60) are clearly stated, the effectiveness of computational sectioning (C61) is demonstrated in Figure 5C vs 5D, and the magnification comparison (C62) is shown in Figure 5E-F.

results.result: Using ELEPHANT for cell detection in the mouse brain cortex achieved 99.4% precision and 97.6% recall, yielding a calculated cell density of 1.18×10⁵ cells/mm³, which closely matches previous reports.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C65 describe the cell detection analysis using ELEPHANT (Figure 5G-I). The precision/recall metrics (C64) are based on manual validation of ~640 cells as described in methods, and the calculated density (C65) is validated by comparison to prior literature (Herculano-Houzel and Lent, 2005).

results.result: Time-lapse 3D imaging of tie1:H2B-eYFP quail embryo from 36 hr (HH10) for 25 hr captured 4200 layers (21 layers × 200 timepoints, 12 µm spacing, 7.5 min intervals) at 113 mW/cm² with 1 s exposure, generating ~500 GB data. The embryo developed normally without phototoxicity/photobleaching. Cell detection identified ~4.5×10⁶ cells across all timepoints, with ~4.0×10⁵ cells tracked, revealing significant changes in high meandering index distribution between t=8 hr and t=16 hr.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C73 describe the quail embryo time-lapse experiment shown in Figure 6. All experimental parameters (C66-C68, C70) are explicitly stated, the lack of phototoxicity (C69) is an important control observation, and the cell detection/tracking results (C71-C72) with dynamic analysis (C73) are demonstrated in Figure 6F-G.

results.result: AMATERAS-2's FOV-to-resolution ratio surpasses previous large-FOV methods, with an optical invariant of 2.75 and space-bandwidth product of 4.3×10⁸, both significantly outperforming earlier studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 present quantitative performance metrics with appropriate citations to the formulas used (Bumstead et al., 2018; Lohmann et al., 1996) and comparisons to prior work. The calculations are based on measured parameters and the comparisons are appropriately cited.

results.result: AMATERAS-2w and -2c achieve spatial resolution of ~1.1-1.8 µm (xy) and 13-16 µm (z), representing significant enhancement over AMATERAS-1 (2.3 and 64 µm). The improved transverse resolution enables clearer visualization of intracellular filamentous structures, and the >4× longitudinal resolution improvement demonstrates the expected effect of >2× NA increase.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81 summarize the measured spatial resolution improvements across both systems (Figures 2, 3) and compare to AMATERAS-1. The improvements match theoretical predictions (C23-C25) and are validated by the filamentous actin imaging (Figure 2F). The >4× z-resolution improvement is consistent with the NA² relationship.

results.result: Volumetric imaging of 1.5-mm-thick mouse brain section was achieved using multipoint-scanning confocal, computational sectioning, and tissue-clearing with 1 s exposure per image and <10 min total acquisition. This could significantly reduce whole-brain acquisition time compared to light-sheet imaging and block-face serial microscopy tomography which require ≥half a day due to narrow FOV tiling.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C85 describe the brain imaging achievement and compare acquisition speed to alternative methods with appropriate citations (Susaki et al., 2014; Seiriki et al., 2019). The speed advantage is logical given the large FOV eliminating tiling requirements, though C85 is prospective for whole-brain extension.

results.result: AMATERAS-2 successfully performed time-lapse observation of centimeter-sized vascular networks in quail embryo, representing the first demonstration of extensive vascular network dynamics throughout the quail embryo at single-cell level and serving as a promising tool for understanding multicellular behavior and tissue formation mechanisms during development.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88 describe the quail embryo application and its significance. The capability (C86) is demonstrated in Figure 6, the novelty claim (C88) is reasonable given the unprecedented scale and resolution, and the potential applications (C87) are appropriately cited (Sasai, 2013; McDole et al., 2018; Dominguez et al., 2023).

results.result: AMATERAS-2 was applied to a 1.2 cm-wide mouse brain section observing various regions with sub-cellular resolution in a single FOV, and performed >24 hr time-lapse imaging of a 1-cm-wide vascular network during quail embryo development, visualizing movement of >4.0×10⁵ vascular endothelial cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6 from the abstract summarize the two major biological applications that are detailed and validated in the Results section (mouse brain: C58-C65, Figure 5; quail embryo: C66-C73, Figure 6). Both applications successfully demonstrate the system's capabilities.

results.result: Multicellular systems are complex and heterogeneous, requiring simultaneous observation of all components to understand cooperative mechanisms, especially when rare cells influence populations or distant cells operate synchronously. Large FOV imaging methods have been developed, mostly for neuroscience using two-photon fluorescence. AMATERAS-1 enabled 10⁵-10⁶ cell observation and detected <1% rare cells triggering transitions in Dictyostelium, but its NA of 0.12 was insufficient for volumetric observation due to broad depth of field.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C14 provide background context and motivation with appropriate citations. The scientific rationale (C7-C9) is well-established, the prior work summary (C10-C13) is appropriately cited, and the limitation of AMATERAS-1 (C14) motivates the current work.

results.result: Conventional microscopy methods selecting limited observation areas have difficulty determining distribution and synchronicity of cellular dynamics across entire systems. The raw data for mouse brain and quail embryo imaging amounted to ~100 GB and ~500 GB respectively, but after processing resulted in several terabytes per experiment.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C92 discuss limitations of conventional methods and data management challenges. The limitation statement (C89) is reasonable background, and the data sizes (C90-C92) are explicitly stated and represent important practical considerations for the technique.

results.result: AMATERAS-2 is a volumetric trans-scale imaging system with an ultra-large field-of-view (1.5×1.0 cm²) and high spatial resolution (~1.1 µm transverse), built using a custom-made giant lens system (NA=0.25, ×2 magnification) and high-megapixel CMOS cameras. The system's optical invariant (2.75) and space-bandwidth product (4.3×10⁸) significantly outperform previously reported large-FOV imaging methods.
results.evaluation: The editor describes this as an 'important study' that 'established a large-scale objective and integrated multiple optical microscopy systems.' Reviewers acknowledge the authors 'have accomplished building such a system, with a field of view of 1.5x1.0 cm2 and a resolution of up to 1.2 um,' confirming the core technical specifications and performance metrics.

results.result: AMATERAS-2 achieves measured transverse resolutions of 1.24±0.12 µm (120-megapixel camera) and 1.12±0.072 µm (250-megapixel camera), with depth of field measurements of 15.6±1.3 µm and 14.8±1.1 µm respectively. This represents approximately two-fold improvement in transverse resolution and more than four-fold improvement in longitudinal resolution compared to AMATERAS-1, enabling clearer visualization of intracellular filamentous structures.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge the system's resolution achievements, stating the authors 'enhanced the system's resolution and sensitivity by increasing the numerical aperture (NA) of the lens.' The editor notes the 'convincing imaging data' across applications. No concerns were raised about the resolution measurements themselves.

results.result: The 3D resolving capability was achieved through optical sectioning using a custom-designed multipoint-scanning confocal system with a pinhole array disk (6 µm pinhole size, 24 µm spacing). The pinhole-array disk dramatically suppressed background light from outside the focal plane, achieving longitudinal FWHM of approximately 16 µm (×1 relay) and 14 µm (×2 relay), though these values exceed the ideal ~9.5 µm due to relatively loose focusing and non-negligible pinhole size.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 raises significant concerns: 'To be used as a volumetric imaging technique, the authors only showcase the implementation of multi-focal confocal sectioning. On the other hand, most of the real biological samples were acquired under the wide-field illumination.' Reviewer 3 notes 'the manuscript lacks a direct comparison for computational sectioning and does not provide a clear evaluation of axial resolution before and after applying computational sectioning,' requesting more direct visual demonstrations.

results.result: A computational sectioning method was developed that estimates out-of-focus contributions by iteratively applying low-pass filtering, assuming higher spatial frequency in the focal plane. After computational sectioning, the distribution of cellular structures in each z-layer is clearly visualized, and clear images were obtained even in areas with strong background light. The method is effective when fluorescent molecules are localized or exhibit filament-like structures.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 expresses concern that 'sometimes I felt that the images were oversharpened and the quantitative nature of these fluorescence images may be perturbed.' Reviewer 3 specifically requests 'more direct visual demonstrations of computational sectioning, along with comparisons of axial resolution before and after applying computational sectioning' and notes 'the manuscript lacks a direct comparison for computational sectioning.' The validation approach is questioned as insufficient.

results.result: AMATERAS-2 successfully performed volumetric imaging of a 1.5-mm-thick mouse brain coronal section using tissue-clearing (CUBIC), acquiring 378 layers in less than 10 minutes. Cell detection using ELEPHANT achieved 99.4% precision and 97.6% recall, yielding a cell density of 1.18×10⁵ cells/mm³ that matches previous reports. The method can significantly reduce acquisition time compared to light-sheet imaging and block-face serial microscopy tomography.
results.evaluation: The editor describes the 'convincing imaging data' covering 'mouse brains' among other applications. Reviewers acknowledge the system was 'demonstrated...on samples such as organoids, brain sections, and embryos.' While concerns exist about computational sectioning validation, the successful application to brain imaging itself is not disputed.

results.result: Time-lapse 3D imaging of quail embryo vascular development was performed for 25 hours, acquiring z-stacks every 7.5 minutes (21 layers, 12 µm spacing) with 1 s exposure at 113 mW/cm² excitation. The embryo developed normally without phototoxicity. Approximately 4.5×10⁶ cells were detected and 4.0×10⁵ cells were tracked across 200 time points, representing the first demonstration of extensive vascular network dynamics throughout the quail embryo at single-cell level.
results.evaluation: The editor notes the work 'will appeal to biologists and imaging technologists focused on long-term imaging of large fields.' However, Reviewer 3 identifies a critical gap: 'The manuscript currently omits critical details about the method's volume imaging rate. In the description of the quail embryo imaging experiment, key parameters such as exposure time and imaging speed are missing.' The reviewer emphasizes 'volume imaging rate is an essential factor for biological researchers to evaluate the applicability of the technique.'

results.result: The imaging system enables observation of subcellular structures such as myofibrils in large-area cell sheets, and the improved transverse resolution enables clearer visualization of intracellular filamentous structures.
results.evaluation: The editor notes the work demonstrates 'potential for long-term imaging of the developmental process' with 'convincing imaging data.' Reviewers acknowledge the system's performance on biological samples including organoids. The capability to resolve subcellular structures is implicitly accepted through the acknowledgment of the resolution improvements.

results.result: Based on the doubled NA (0.25 vs 0.12), AMATERAS-2 in principle achieves over twice the spatial resolution in the transverse direction, more than four times the resolution in the longitudinal direction, and over four times the brightness compared to AMATERAS-1.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge 'the authors enhanced the system's resolution and sensitivity by increasing the numerical aperture (NA) of the lens.' The theoretical improvements based on NA are standard optical principles and are not challenged. The measured improvements (C78-C81) confirm these theoretical predictions.

results.result: Alternative 3D imaging approaches were considered but deemed unsuitable: light-sheet microscopy struggles with uniform illumination over centimeter-scale FOV, light-field microscopy involves incompatible trade-offs between spatial resolution and 3D capability, and two-photon microscopy requires further innovations in laser power and scanning for wide FOV application.
results.evaluation: These justifications for the chosen approach are presented with supporting citations and are not challenged by reviewers. The rationale for selecting the confocal approach is implicitly accepted through the reviewers' focus on implementation details rather than the fundamental choice of method.

results.result: The raw data for 3D imaging of mouse brain section and time-lapse 3D imaging of quail embryo amounted to approximately 100 GB and 500 GB respectively, with single experimental measurements resulting in several terabytes after multiple image processing and analysis steps.
results.evaluation: These data volume descriptions are factual statements about the experimental outputs and are not disputed by reviewers. The large data volumes are consistent with the high-resolution, large-FOV nature of the system that reviewers acknowledge.

results.result: Background and motivation claims establishing the scientific context: multicellular systems are complex and heterogeneous, requiring simultaneous observation of all components; conventional microscopy methods have difficulty determining distribution and synchronicity across entire systems; previous large-FOV methods focused mainly on neuroscience; AMATERAS-1 had limitations including insufficient NA (0.12) for volumetric observation.
results.evaluation: These are background and contextual claims supported by citations. Reviewer 3 notes 'this paper is just a minor improvement of the authors' previous work,' implicitly acknowledging the prior AMATERAS-1 system and its limitations. The scientific motivation is not challenged by reviewers.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on theoretical optical predictions (C23-C25). Both find these standard optical relationships well-supported. OpenEval notes experimental validation in later claims, while peer reviewers acknowledge the NA-based resolution enhancements without challenge.

Strong agreement on background and contextual claims (C7-C14, C89). Both evaluations find these well-supported with appropriate citations. Peer reviewer implicitly acknowledges AMATERAS-1 limitations by noting this work is 'a minor improvement' of previous work.

Significant disagreement on computational sectioning validation (C52-C57, C61). OpenEval finds the method 'clearly explained' with results 'demonstrated in Figure 4D-E' and limitations 'appropriately stated.' Peer reviewers express concern about oversharpening, lack of direct comparisons, and insufficient quantitative validation of axial resolution improvements.

Agreement on data volume claims (C90-C92). Both evaluations find these factual statements about experimental outputs well-supported and consistent with the high-resolution, large-FOV system characteristics.

Disagreement on confocal system implementation (C45-C51). OpenEval finds the design well-documented with 'dramatic background suppression visually demonstrated' and measured PSF characteristics with N=100. Peer reviewers raise concerns about limited use of confocal sectioning in biological samples and request more direct demonstrations of computational sectioning effectiveness.

Partial disagreement on quail embryo experiment (C66-C73, C86-C88). OpenEval finds all experimental parameters 'explicitly stated' and results well-demonstrated. Peer reviewers acknowledge the application but identify critical missing details about volume imaging rate, exposure time, and imaging speed essential for evaluating biological applicability.

Agreement on confocal approach rationale (C40-C42). Both evaluations find the justification for choosing the confocal method well-supported with appropriate citations. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this through focus on implementation rather than fundamental method choice.

Agreement on optical specifications (C15-C22, plus system specs C1-C3, C26-C27, C74-C77). Both evaluations confirm these technical specifications are well-documented. Peer reviewers acknowledge the system was 'accomplished' with stated FOV and resolution, and editor describes it as 'important study.'

Agreement on measured PSF characteristics and resolution (C26-C34, C28-C29, C32-C33). Both evaluations support the experimental measurements. OpenEval notes N=100 measurements with error bars; peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge resolution enhancements and provide 'convincing imaging data' assessment.

Agreement on spatial resolution improvements (C78-C81). Both evaluations confirm the measured improvements match theoretical predictions. Peer reviewers acknowledge the enhanced resolution and sensitivity through increased NA without disputing the quantitative claims.

Agreement on brain imaging achievement (C82-C85, C5, C58-C65). Both evaluations support the successful application to mouse brain imaging. Editor notes 'convincing imaging data' and reviewers acknowledge demonstration on brain sections. Concerns about computational sectioning validation exist separately but don't dispute the brain imaging capability itself.

Agreement on mouse brain imaging experiment parameters (C58-C60, C62). Both evaluations find the experimental setup well-documented. OpenEval notes parameters are 'clearly stated'; peer reviewers acknowledge the brain imaging application without disputing these specific claims.

Agreement on cell detection analysis (C63-C65). OpenEval finds the ELEPHANT-based analysis with manual validation of ~640 cells well-supported. Peer reviewers acknowledge the brain imaging results without challenging the cell detection methodology or density calculations.

Partial agreement on quail embryo significance (C86-C88). OpenEval finds the capability demonstrated and novelty claim reasonable. Peer reviewers acknowledge potential for 'long-term imaging of developmental process' but note missing critical details about imaging rates that affect evaluation of biological applicability.

Agreement on quantitative performance metrics (C74-C77). Both evaluations support these calculations based on measured parameters with appropriate citations. Peer reviewers acknowledge the system specifications that underlie these metrics.

Agreement on practical imaging improvements (C36-C39). OpenEval finds the 2× improvement matching theoretical predictions with visual demonstration. Peer reviewers acknowledge resolution enhancements and provide overall positive assessment of imaging data quality.

Agreement on subcellular resolution capability (C39, C80). Both evaluations support the ability to resolve subcellular structures. OpenEval notes sharper features in filamentous actin imaging; peer reviewers implicitly accept this through acknowledgment of resolution improvements.

Agreement on core system specifications (C1-C4). Both evaluations confirm the technical specifications are well-documented. Peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge the 1.5×1.0 cm² FOV and up to 1.2 μm resolution, confirming the system was successfully built.

Agreement on mouse brain application summary (C5). Both evaluations support this abstract claim as validated by detailed results. Editor notes 'convincing imaging data' for mouse brains; OpenEval notes it's demonstrated in Figure 5.

Partial agreement on quail embryo application summary (C6). Both acknowledge the demonstration but peer reviewers identify missing critical details about imaging rates that affect full evaluation of the time-lapse capability claims.
